paragraphs.text: This review explains a math tool for studying how groups of brain cells, or neurons, combine the signals they receive. The tool is called partial information decomposition, or PID, and the authors also describe their own studies using it.

paragraphs.text: How brains turn senses into useful behavior is a grand challenge of neuroscience, and it remains poorly understood. Recording tools can now capture hundreds or thousands of neurons at once, but ways to make sense of that data have lagged behind.

paragraphs.text: PID splits what two input neurons tell us about a third into three kinds: shared by both, unique to one, or synergistic. Synergistic means it shows up only in the two inputs' combined pattern, never in either alone. In mouse brain tissue, trios inside a "rich club", a tight group of the best-connected neurons, had 2.7 times more synergy. Trios whose two input neurons were linked to each other in both directions had 50% more synergy than trios with neither link.

paragraphs.text: In monkeys, shared information rose sharply during movement, perhaps so the "move" signal arrives reliably. The authors conclude that neurons do not just add up inputs; they respond to patterns, shaped by their surroundings and by behavior. PID finds these patterns but does not yet explain the biology that causes them.

fuller.text: How brains turn sensory signals into useful behavior is a grand challenge, and it remains poorly understood. New recording methods now capture hundreds or thousands of neurons at once, but researchers still need ways to make sense of the data. Simply tracking how information flows from one neuron to another cannot show how several input streams interact.

fuller.text: PID splits what two input neurons tell us about a target neuron into three kinds. Redundant information comes from either input, unique information from only one, and synergistic information only from both inputs' pattern together. The authors treat synergy as a sign that the target is doing real computation on its inputs.

fuller.text: In slices of mouse cortex grown in a dish, tightly linked hubs of neurons called "rich clubs" showed 2.7 times more synergy than other groups. Groups where the two inputs were also linked to each other had up to 50% more synergy. In monkeys, redundancy rose sharply during reaching movements, perhaps to send the "move" signal reliably.

brief.text: This review explains a math tool for studying how brain cells handle information. The tool splits the information a cell gets from several input cells into separate kinds. How brain circuits actually process information is one of the biggest open questions in brain science.

sentences.text: This review explains a math tool for studying how brain cells handle information.
The tool splits the information a cell gets from several input cells into separate kinds.
How brain circuits actually process information is one of the biggest open questions in brain science.

brief.text: The key idea is synergy: information that shows up only when several inputs are read together. Studies in mouse brain tissue and in monkeys found synergy is common in brain circuits. It was highest among the most tightly linked groups of cells. So cells seem not to just add up their inputs; they also respond to patterns in them.
